Fun Fact Friday: Did you know that the idea of “majors” in colleges and universities as we know them was originally pressed by Robert E. Lee in his position as President of Washington College (later Washington and Lee University) following the Civil War? Why might that be?

When Lee first came to Lexington, one of the most pressing issues was the desperate need to begin rebuilding the South and the entire country. In an age when a typical college student’s course of study consisted primarily of subjects such as ancient languages, history, and philosophy, students were much more prepared to practice law, politics, or enter the ministry than anything else. The nation needed individuals practiced in topics such as science, math, agriculture, and engineering to help realistically rebuild an entire country!

So, President Lee made a very important decision: expand the curriculum and let the students decide what they wanted to study and later pursue within a wider range of career choices. The elective system was born. It was a couple years later when the next president of a higher education institution would first declare that “the young man of nineteen or twenty ought to know what he likes best and is most fit for.” That man was Charles W. Eliot of Harvard University.

And remember, if you want to learn more beyond today’s #FunFactFriday about Robert E. Lee’s long-lasting and forward-thinking contributions in the field of education, be sure to pick up David Cox’s book “Lee Chapel at 150: A History” – there’s always more to learn where this came from!
